params.question: In the WHO xerophthalmia staging system, at which stage should a primary health centre refer the child for urgent specialist care?

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Night blindness (XN) is the earliest sign and responds well to oral vitamin A at a primary health centre. Referral is triggered only when the cornea becomes involved.

Bitot's spots are foamy deposits on the temporal bulbar conjunctiva — a conjunctival sign, not a corneal one. The corneas remain clear at this stage, and vitamin A supplementation at a PHC is sufficient.

Correct. X2 marks corneal involvement. Once the cornea is dry, permanent damage including keratomalacia and perforation can follow within hours. Stages XN through X1B respond to vitamin A at a PHC; X2 and beyond require urgent specialist referral.

answers.text: X3B — Keratomalacia of one-third or more of the cornea

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: X3B represents advanced keratomalacia with perforation risk. Referral should have occurred much earlier — at X2 (corneal xerosis) — to prevent this stage from developing.

overallFeedback.feedback: The cornea is the dividing line. Stages XN through X1B (conjunctival signs) can be managed with vitamin A at a PHC. X2 (corneal xerosis) and beyond require urgent specialist referral to prevent permanent blindness.
X2 (corneal xerosis) is the critical referral threshold. The cornea is the dividing line between PHC-manageable and specialist-urgent disease.

interactions.label: Why are alkali chemical burns to the eye more destructive than acid burns?

params.question: Why are alkali chemical burns to the eye more destructive than acid burns?

answers.text: Acid denatures surface proteins into a barrier that limits penetration, whereas alkali dissolves cell membranes and penetrates continuously

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Correct. Acid causes coagulative necrosis — denatured proteins form a barrier limiting depth of penetration. Alkali causes liquefactive necrosis — it dissolves cell membranes with no barrier formation, penetrating through the cornea into the anterior chamber until the chemical is completely irrigated away.

answers.text: Alkali causes coagulative necrosis that destroys tissue more rapidly than acid

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: This reverses the mechanisms. Coagulative necrosis is the acid pattern, not alkali. Alkali causes liquefactive necrosis — continuous penetration with no protective protein barrier.

answers.text: Alkali reacts exothermically with the tear film, generating heat that thermally damages the cornea

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: The greater destructiveness of alkali is due to its necrosis pattern, not heat generation. Liquefactive necrosis allows unlimited depth of penetration, unlike the self-limiting coagulative necrosis caused by acid.

answers.text: Alkali selectively destroys the lacrimal gland, preventing natural tear clearance of the chemical

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: The key difference is the necrosis pattern. Alkali causes liquefactive necrosis, dissolving cell membranes and penetrating continuously into deeper structures without forming a protective barrier.

overallFeedback.feedback: Acid causes coagulative necrosis (denatured proteins form a barrier, self-limiting). Alkali causes liquefactive necrosis (dissolves membranes, no barrier, penetrates continuously). This is why irrigation must begin immediately — every minute of delay allows deeper alkali penetration.

Alkali's liquefactive necrosis dissolves cell membranes without forming a barrier, allowing continuous penetration — which is exactly why immediate, copious irrigation is the single most important first action in any chemical eye burn.

params.question: A patient presents with a blind, painful eye and no tumour is visible on clinical examination. The surgeon considers evisceration for pain relief. What must be done before proceeding, and why?

answers.text: Fluorescein angiography to confirm vascular status, because ischaemic eyes heal poorly after evisceration

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: The critical concern before evisceration is not vascular status but the possibility of a hidden intraocular tumour. B-scan ultrasonography is mandatory — a blind, painful eye can conceal a melanoma that alters the surgical plan entirely.

answers.text: MRI of the orbits to evaluate the optic nerve, because optic nerve involvement would necessitate exenteration

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: MRI is not the standard pre-evisceration investigation and is contraindicated if a metallic intraocular foreign body is suspected. B-scan ultrasound is mandatory to exclude a hidden intraocular mass.

answers.text: Visual evoked potentials to confirm complete blindness, because residual vision contraindicates globe removal

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: While confirming blindness matters, the mandatory pre-evisceration step is B-scan ultrasonography. A blind painful eye can conceal an intraocular melanoma — and if a tumour is present, the procedure must change from evisceration to enucleation.

answers.text: B-scan ultrasonography to exclude a hidden intraocular mass, because tumour cells can escape through scleral emissary canals if the sclera is left intact

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Correct. B-scan before evisceration is non-negotiable. Evisceration leaves the scleral shell intact, and the sclera contains emissary canals — tiny channels through which tumour cells can escape into the orbit. If B-scan reveals a mass, enucleation (removing the entire globe) is mandatory.

overallFeedback.feedback: B-scan ultrasonography is mandatory before evisceration. A blind painful eye can hide a melanoma. If a tumour is found, enucleation — not evisceration — is required, because evisceration leaves the sclera intact and its emissary canals allow tumour cells to escape into the orbit.

B-scan before evisceration is a critical safeguard. The scleral emissary canals are the anatomical reason — leaving the sclera in place when a tumour is present leaves the escape route open for orbital spread.

interactions.label: India's National Programme for Control of Blindness (NPCB, 1976) was renamed NPC

params.question: India's National Programme for Control of Blindness (NPCB, 1976) was renamed NPCBVI in 2017. What does the expanded name signify?

answers.text: The programme now focuses exclusively on childhood blindness prevention through vitamin A supplementation

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: The programme always included vitamin A supplementation. The name change reflects a broader scope — covering all levels of visual impairment, not narrowing to one intervention or age group.

answers.text: The programme now covers all grades of visual impairment, not blindness alone

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Correct. Adding 'Visual Impairment' reflects a mandate expanded beyond blindness (acuity below 3/60) to include mild, moderate, and severe visual impairment — recognising that sub-blindness vision loss also significantly affects daily function and productivity.

answers.text: The programme was merged with India's national disability programme to create a unified service

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: NPCBVI remains a distinct programme under the Ministry of Health. The name change signifies its own expanded scope — from blindness alone to all visual impairment — not a merger with another programme.

answers.text: The programme shifted from curative surgery to purely preventive community interventions

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: NPCBVI continues to provide both curative services (free cataract surgery with IOL implantation) and preventive activities (vitamin A supplementation, school eye screening). The name change reflects broadened scope, not a shift away from surgery.

overallFeedback.feedback: The 2017 renaming from NPCB to NPCBVI broadened the programme's mandate from blindness alone to all visual impairment — mild, moderate, and severe. The programme continues to deliver both preventive and curative services.

The 'VI' addition signals a shift from addressing blindness alone to covering the full spectrum of visual impairment — aligning with WHO data showing 2.2 billion people globally have some form of vision impairment.
